tool.name: Tailwind CSS
tool.tagline: Utility-first CSS framework: style by composing small classes in your markup
tool.description: Tailwind CSS provides thousands of small single-purpose classes such as flex, pt-4 and text-center that you combine directly in HTML or components. Version 4 is configured in CSS with @theme, builds on native cascade layers and CSS variables, and detects the classes you use automatically. It's one of the most popular ways to style React, Vue, Svelte and server-rendered apps quickly and consistently.

concepts.name: Installing Tailwind v4
concepts.summary: Add Tailwind v4 to a project with the Vite plugin, PostCSS or the CLI, and import it with a single @import line.
concepts.why: Version 4 setup is much simpler than v3, and older tutorials with tailwind.config.js no longer match.
concepts.body:
Tailwind is a build step: it scans your source files for class names and generates a CSS file containing only the utilities you use.

In v4 there's no required JavaScript config and no `@tailwind` directives. Setup is two pieces.

- **An integration.** With Vite (React, Vue, Svelte, Astro and more), install `tailwindcss` and `@tailwindcss/vite` and add the plugin to `vite.config`. Other tools use the PostCSS plugin `@tailwindcss/postcss`. With no bundler at all, the standalone CLI works: `npx @tailwindcss/cli -i input.css -o output.css --watch`. Frameworks such as Next.js and Laravel document their own one-step setup.
- **One CSS import.** In your main stylesheet, write `@import "tailwindcss";`. This pulls in the theme variables, the Preflight base styles and all utilities.

Then use classes in your markup, and the dev server rebuilds as you type. **Content detection** is automatic: Tailwind scans your project, skipping files in `.gitignore`, binary files and CSS files, so there's no `content` array to maintain.

Install the official editor extension (Tailwind CSS IntelliSense) for autocompletion, hover previews of the generated CSS and lint warnings, and the Prettier plugin `prettier-plugin-tailwindcss` to sort classes in a consistent order.

Tailwind v4 targets modern browsers only: Safari 16.4+, Chrome 111+ and Firefox 128+. If you must support older ones, stay on v3.4.
takeaways: v4 setup = an integration (Vite, PostCSS or CLI) + @import "tailwindcss"
Class detection is automatic, no content array
Install IntelliSense and the Prettier class-sorting plugin
v4 needs Safari 16.4+, Chrome 111+, Firefox 128+
pitfalls: Following a v3 tutorial with @tailwind base/components/utilities and tailwind.config.js content paths.

quiz.q: What replaces the three @tailwind directives of v3 in a v4 stylesheet?
options: Nothing; v4 needs no CSS file
quiz.explain: A single @import brings in theme, base styles and utilities.

concepts.name: The utility-first workflow
concepts.summary: Style elements by combining small single-purpose classes in the markup instead of writing custom CSS rules.
concepts.why: Understanding the trade-offs explains why Tailwind code looks the way it does and when it pays off.
concepts.body:
In traditional CSS you invent a class name, `.profile-card`, and write its rules in a stylesheet. In Tailwind you compose **utility classes**, each doing one thing, right in the markup:

```html
<div class="mx-auto max-w-sm rounded-xl bg-white p-6 shadow-lg">
```

`p-6` is padding, `rounded-xl` is border radius, `shadow-lg` is a box shadow. Every utility maps to one or a few CSS declarations from a shared design scale.

Why people like it:

- No naming and no context switching between files.
- Styles are local: changing a class affects only that element, so there's no fear of breaking a distant page.
- CSS stops growing, because the same utilities are reused everywhere and unused ones are never generated.
- Design constraints: spacing, colours and font sizes come from one scale, which keeps the UI consistent.

The common objections have answers. Long class lists are handled by extracting **components** in your framework (a `Card` component, a template partial), not by writing CSS. It's not inline styles: utilities support hover, focus, responsive and dark variants, which inline styles can't.

Preflight, Tailwind's base layer, resets browser defaults: headings and paragraphs lose their margins and font sizes, and lists lose bullets. That's intentional, so every visual style is explicit; add utilities, or style rich text with the typography plugin.

takeaways: Each utility does one thing from a shared design scale
Reuse through components, not custom class names

concepts.name: Spacing and sizing
concepts.summary: Use the spacing scale for padding, margin, gap, width and height, including fractions, size-*, and dynamic values like p-13.
concepts.why: Spacing and sizing utilities are the classes you'll type most.
concepts.body:
Tailwind v4 derives every spacing utility from one variable, `--spacing`, which is `0.25rem` (4px) by default. A number is a multiple of it: `p-4` is `calc(var(--spacing) * 4)`, 1rem. Any integer works, so `p-13` or `mt-17` are valid without configuration.

**Padding and margin**: `p-4` (all sides), `px-4`/`py-2` (horizontal/vertical), `pt-2`, `pr-3`, `pb-4`, `pl-5`, and logical `ps-4`/`pe-4` (start/end, for right-to-left support). Margins mirror them with `m-`, plus `mx-auto` for centering and negative margins like `-mt-2`.

**Gaps**: `gap-4`, `gap-x-2`, `gap-y-6` in flex and grid. Prefer gap over margins between siblings. (`space-y-4` adds margins between children if you're not in flex or grid.)

**Width and height**:

- scale values: `w-64`, `h-10`,
- fractions: `w-1/2`, `w-2/3`,
- keywords: `w-full` (100%), `w-screen` (100vw), `h-dvh`, `w-fit`, `w-min`, `w-max`,
- both at once: `size-10` sets width and height.

**Constraints**: `max-w-prose` (65ch), `max-w-md` and friends from the container scale (`max-w-md` is 28rem), `min-h-dvh`, `min-w-0`.

`p-px` gives 1px and `p-0.5` half a step. For values off the scale, the arbitrary syntax `w-[37px]` exists (covered later), but reach for the scale first; it's what keeps a design consistent.

Content

Readable line length.
takeaways: Numbers are multiples of --spacing (0.25rem): p-4 = 1rem
Any integer works without config: p-13
size-* sets width and height together
Prefer gap over margins between siblings
pitfalls: Using space-y-* on a flex or grid container where gap-* is simpler and more robust.

concepts.name: Colours and typography
concepts.summary: Apply the colour palette with text-, bg- and border- utilities and opacity modifiers, and set type with size, weight and leading utilities.
concepts.why: Colour and type utilities make up most of a component's visual style.
concepts.body:
**Colours** come from a default palette of more than twenty hues (red, orange, amber, yellow, green, emerald, teal, sky, blue, indigo, violet, purple, pink, rose and others, plus several grays such as slate, gray, zinc and stone), each with shades from `50` (lightest) to `950` (darkest), defined in **oklch**. Use them with any colour utility:

- `text-gray-700`, `bg-indigo-600`, `border-red-500`, `ring-blue-500`, `fill-current`, `decoration-sky-400`,
- plus `black`, `white`, `transparent` and `current` (currentColor).

The **opacity modifier** adds alpha with a slash: `bg-black/50`, `text-white/80`, `border-gray-900/10`. It works on every colour utility, replacing v3's separate `bg-opacity-*` classes.

**Typography**:

- size: `text-xs`, `text-sm`, `text-base` (1rem), `text-lg` up to `text-9xl`. Each size comes with a matching default line height.
- line height override in the same class: `text-lg/7` (size lg, leading 7 spacing units), or separately `leading-tight`, `leading-6`.
- weight: `font-normal`, `font-medium`, `font-semibold`, `font-bold`.
- family: `font-sans`, `font-serif`, `font-mono`.
- `tracking-tight`, `uppercase`, `italic`, `underline`, `truncate` (single line with ellipsis), `line-clamp-3`, `text-balance` for nicer headings, `text-center`.

Choose shades with contrast in mind: `text-gray-500` on white is fine for secondary text, but lighter grays usually fail WCAG for body copy.
concepts.code:
Release notes

Faster builds in version 4

The new engine is up to 5x faster for full builds.

Read the changelog
Tip: bg-black/50 means black at 50% opacity.
takeaways: Shades run 50 (light) to 950 (dark) on every hue
A slash adds opacity to any colour: bg-black/50
text-lg/7 sets font size and line height together
Check contrast for text colours
pitfalls: Using v3's bg-opacity-50 class, which v4 removed; use bg-black/50.

quiz.q: Which class gives a red-500 border at 25% opacity?
quiz.explain: The slash modifier sets alpha on that one colour; opacity-25 would fade the whole element.

concepts.name: Flexbox and grid layouts
concepts.summary: Build layouts with flex, items-center, justify-between, grid-cols-* and col-span-* utilities.
concepts.why: Layout utilities let you build navbars, card grids and page shells without leaving the markup.
concepts.body:
Tailwind's layout utilities map directly onto CSS flexbox and grid.

**Flexbox**:

- `flex` (or `inline-flex`), `flex-col` for a column, `flex-wrap`.
- Alignment: `items-center`, `items-start`, `justify-between`, `justify-center`, `self-end`.
- Item sizing: `flex-1` (grow and shrink, basis 0), `flex-auto`, `flex-none`, `grow`, `shrink-0`, `basis-64`.
- `gap-4` between items, `order-first` to reorder.

**Grid**:

- `grid` with `grid-cols-3` creates three equal columns. The generated CSS is `repeat(3, minmax(0, 1fr))`, so columns can shrink below their content's width without overflowing.
- `col-span-2` spans two columns; `col-span-full` spans all; `col-start-2` places explicitly.
- `grid-rows-*`, `row-span-*`, `grid-flow-col`, `auto-rows-fr`.
- `place-items-center` centers content in each cell.

Centering anything takes three classes: `flex items-center justify-center`, or `grid place-items-center`.

A common page shell: `grid min-h-dvh grid-rows-[auto_1fr_auto]` for header, content and footer. A sidebar layout: `flex` on the wrapper, `w-64 shrink-0` on the sidebar and `min-w-0 flex-1` on the content, where `min-w-0` keeps long content from overflowing.

Layout classes combine with responsive prefixes: `grid-cols-1 md:grid-cols-3` is one column on phones and three on wider screens.

grid-cols-N uses minmax(0, 1fr) columns
col-span-* and col-span-full place grid items
flex-1 + min-w-0 for content that must shrink

concepts.name: Hover, focus and other states
concepts.summary: Apply utilities conditionally with variants like hover:, focus-visible:, disabled:, group-hover:, peer-checked: and has-*.
concepts.why: Variants are how utility classes handle interaction states that inline styles never could.
concepts.body:
A **variant** is a prefix that applies a utility only under a condition: `hover:bg-indigo-700` sets the background only on hover. Variants exist for nearly every pseudo-class:

- interaction: `hover:`, `focus:`, `focus-visible:`, `active:`, `focus-within:`,
- forms: `disabled:`, `checked:`, `required:`, `invalid:`, `user-invalid:`, `placeholder:` (the pseudo-element), `file:`,
- structure: `first:`, `last:`, `odd:`, `even:`, `nth-3:`, `not-first:`, `empty:`,
- `open:` for details and dialogs, `before:`/`after:` for pseudo-elements, `aria-expanded:` and `data-[state=open]:` for attributes.

In v4, `hover:` is wrapped in `@media (hover: hover)`, so tapping on a touch screen doesn't leave sticky hover styles.

**Styling based on other elements**:

- Mark a parent with `group`, then use `group-hover:` or `group-focus:` on any descendant.
- Mark a sibling with `peer` and use `peer-checked:` or `peer-invalid:` on later siblings (it must come *before* them, as with the CSS `~` combinator).
- `has-checked:` and `has-[img]:` use `:has()` to style an element by its contents.
- Name groups to disambiguate nested ones: `group/item` with `group-hover/item:`.

Variants stack: `dark:md:hover:bg-gray-700`. In v4 they apply left to right, like the nested CSS they produce.

takeaways: Prefix any utility with a state: hover:, focus-visible:, disabled:
group/group-* styles children from a parent's state
peer/peer-* styles later siblings; the peer must come first
hover: only applies on devices that can hover
pitfalls: Putting the peer element after the element that uses peer-*; the sibling selector only looks backwards.

options: group on the text, group-checked: on the checkbox
peer on the checkbox, peer-checked: on the text
quiz.explain: peer marks the earlier sibling; peer-checked: applies when it is checked.

concepts.name: Responsive design
concepts.summary: Build mobile-first layouts with sm:, md:, lg:, xl: and 2xl: breakpoint prefixes, plus max-* and range variants.
concepts.why: Responsive prefixes let one set of classes describe the layout for every screen size.
concepts.body:
Breakpoint variants apply a utility from a minimum width upwards:

- `sm:` 40rem (640px)
- `md:` 48rem (768px)
- `lg:` 64rem (1024px)
- `xl:` 80rem (1280px)
- `2xl:` 96rem (1536px)

Tailwind is **mobile-first**: unprefixed classes apply to all sizes, and prefixed ones override from that width up. So `text-center sm:text-left` is centred on phones and left-aligned from 640px. A common mistake is reaching for `sm:` to target phones; the unprefixed class already does that.

To target a range, stack a `max-*` variant: `md:max-lg:flex` applies only between md and lg. `max-md:hidden` hides below 768px.

Breakpoints are theme variables. Add or change them in CSS:

```css
@theme { --breakpoint-3xl: 120rem; }
```

which immediately enables `3xl:` utilities. One-off breakpoints use arbitrary values such as `min-[320px]:text-sm`.

The generated media queries use the modern range syntax (`@media (width >= 48rem)`), in rem, so they respect user font settings.

Good responsive Tailwind usually needs fewer breakpoints than you'd think: `flex-wrap`, `grid-cols-[repeat(auto-fit,minmax(16rem,1fr))]` and fluid widths adapt continuously. Use breakpoints for structural changes, like showing the full navigation from `md:` up.

concepts.name: Dark mode
concepts.summary: Style dark themes with the dark: variant, driven by the system preference or by a class or data attribute you toggle.
concepts.why: Users expect dark mode, and Tailwind makes supporting it a matter of adding dark: classes.
concepts.body:
The `dark:` variant applies a utility when dark mode is active: `bg-white dark:bg-gray-900`.

By default it follows the operating system setting, compiling to `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)`. No JavaScript is needed.

To let users choose, redefine the variant in your CSS so it depends on a class or attribute instead:

```css
@custom-variant dark (&:where(.dark, .dark *));
```

Now `dark:` applies inside any element with the `dark` class, usually `<html class="dark">`. A tiny script in the head sets that class before the page paints (from `localStorage` or `matchMedia`) to avoid a flash of the wrong theme. A data attribute works the same way: `&:where([data-theme=dark], [data-theme=dark] *)`.

Practical advice:

- Design the pairs together: `text-gray-900 dark:text-gray-100`, `border-gray-200 dark:border-white/10`. Translucent whites and blacks (`bg-white/5`) adapt well to layered dark surfaces.
- Set `color-scheme` (the `scheme-light-dark` utility or CSS) so form controls and scrollbars match.
- For larger apps, define semantic colour variables in `@theme` and switch their values in dark mode, then use `bg-surface` and `text-muted` everywhere instead of writing `dark:` pairs on every element.
concepts.code: Card text
takeaways: dark: follows prefers-color-scheme by default
@custom-variant dark (...) switches it to a class or attribute
Set the class in a head script to avoid a flash of the wrong theme
Semantic colour variables beat dark: pairs in large apps
pitfalls: Toggling the dark class after the page has rendered, causing a white flash on load.

quiz.q: Without any configuration, when does dark:bg-black apply in Tailwind v4?
options: Never, dark mode must be enabled in a config file
When the OS or browser prefers a dark colour scheme
quiz.explain: The default dark variant uses the prefers-color-scheme media query.

concepts.name: Customising the theme with @theme
concepts.summary: Define colours, fonts, breakpoints and other design tokens in CSS with @theme, generating utilities and CSS variables at once.
concepts.why: @theme is how every v4 project brings in its own brand, and it replaces most of tailwind.config.js.
concepts.body:
In v4 the design system lives in CSS. **Theme variables** are custom properties declared in an `@theme` block, and their **namespace** decides which utilities they create:

- `--color-brand-500` creates `bg-brand-500`, `text-brand-500`, `border-brand-500` and so on,
- `--font-display` creates `font-display`,
- `--text-*`, `--font-weight-*`, `--leading-*`, `--tracking-*` for type,
- `--breakpoint-*` for responsive variants, `--container-*` for container sizes and `max-w-*`,
- `--radius-*`, `--shadow-*`, `--ease-*`, `--animate-*`, and `--spacing` for the whole spacing scale.

Every theme variable is also emitted as a normal CSS variable on `:root` (when used), so you can read it anywhere: `var(--color-brand-500)` in custom CSS, inline styles or JavaScript.

To **extend**, just add variables. To **override** a default, redeclare it with the same name. To **remove** a whole namespace, set it to `initial` (`--color-*: initial;`) and define only your own colours; `--*: initial` clears the entire default theme.

Use plain `:root` variables for values that shouldn't create utilities. Use `@theme inline` when a theme variable refers to another variable, so utilities use the final value rather than a reference that might resolve differently deeper in the tree.

To share a theme across projects, put the `@theme` block in its own CSS file and `@import` it.
takeaways: @theme variables generate utilities based on their namespace
They're also real CSS variables usable anywhere
Redeclare to override; --color-*: initial removes a namespace
Use :root for variables that shouldn't create utilities
pitfalls: Putting brand colours in :root and wondering why bg-brand-500 doesn't exist.

quiz.q: Which declaration in @theme makes a class like shadow-glow available?

concepts.name: Container queries
concepts.summary: Make components adapt to their parent's width with the @container class and @sm:, @md:, @lg: variants.
concepts.why: Components that respond to their own space can be reused anywhere without page-level breakpoints.
concepts.body:
Container queries are built into Tailwind v4. Two steps:

- Add the `@container` class to a parent, which sets `container-type: inline-size`.
- Use `@`-prefixed variants on descendants: `@md:flex-row` applies when the nearest container is at least `28rem` wide.

The container sizes are separate from screen breakpoints and smaller: `@3xs` (16rem), `@2xs` (18rem), `@xs` (20rem), `@sm` (24rem), `@md` (28rem), `@lg` (32rem), `@xl` (36rem), `@2xl` (42rem) and up to `@7xl` (80rem). They come from the `--container-*` theme variables, which also drive `max-w-md` and friends.

Like screen breakpoints, they're mobile-first, with `@max-md:` for the opposite direction and ranges such as `@sm:@max-md:`.

**Named containers** handle nesting: `@container/sidebar` on the parent and `@lg/sidebar:grid-cols-2` on a child target that container specifically rather than the nearest one.

Arbitrary sizes work too: `@min-[400px]:flex`.

The **cqw** and related units are available through arbitrary values, such as `text-[5cqw]`, for type that scales with the container.

Rule of thumb: screen breakpoints (`md:`) for the page skeleton, container variants (`@md:`) inside reusable components like cards, list items and widgets.

concepts.name: Arbitrary values and properties
concepts.summary: Escape the design scale with square-bracket values like w-[37px], CSS-variable shorthand bg-(--x), and arbitrary properties.
concepts.why: Real designs always have a few one-off values, and this is how you handle them without leaving the markup.
concepts.body:
When the scale doesn't have what you need, put any CSS value in square brackets:

- `w-[37px]`, `top-[117px]`, `bg-[#bada55]`, `grid-cols-[200px_1fr_auto]`.
- Spaces are written as underscores (class names can't contain spaces): `grid-rows-[auto_1fr_auto]`. Write `\_` for a real underscore.
- CSS functions work: `w-[calc(100%-2rem)]`, `h-[min(50vh,30rem)]`.

**CSS variables** have a shorthand with parentheses: `bg-(--brand-color)` compiles to `background-color: var(--brand-color)`. (In v3 this was written `bg-[--brand-color]`.) That's the clean way to pass dynamic values from JavaScript: set `style="--progress: 40%"` on the element and use `w-(--progress)`.

When a value is ambiguous, add a **type hint**: `text-(length:--size)` is a font size, while `text-(color:--accent)` is a colour.

**Arbitrary properties** apply any CSS declaration as a class, with variants still available: `[mask-type:luminance]`, `hover:[mask-type:alpha]`.

**Arbitrary variants** build a selector on the fly: `[&>*]:p-4` styles all direct children, `[&:nth-child(3)]:underline`, and `data-[state=open]:rotate-180`.

Use these sparingly. If the same arbitrary value appears in several places, it belongs in `@theme` as a token. And class names must be complete strings in the source; you can't build `w-[${n}px]` at runtime.

bg-(--var) is shorthand for var(--var)

concepts.name: Custom utilities and variants
concepts.summary: Register your own utilities with @utility (including functional ones with --value()) and your own variants with @custom-variant.
concepts.why: When a pattern repeats across a codebase, a first-class utility or variant keeps markup clean and consistent.
takeaways: @utility adds utilities that work with all variants
Functional utilities use name-* and --value()
@custom-variant defines new variants; @variant uses one inside CSS
@plugin loads JS plugins such as typography
pitfalls: Writing custom utilities as plain classes in @layer utilities, where v4 no longer treats them as variant-aware utilities; use @utility.

concepts.name: Reuse: components, @apply and class merging
concepts.summary: Avoid duplication by extracting framework components, use @apply sparingly, and manage variant classes with helpers like clsx and tailwind-merge.
concepts.why: Long repeated class lists are the main maintenance cost of Tailwind, and these patterns keep it under control.
concepts.body:
The answer to "my class lists repeat" is usually **a component**, not CSS. Put the markup in a React, Vue or Svelte component, a template partial, or even a loop, and the classes exist once.

**Variants of a component** (primary/secondary, sm/lg) are best expressed as maps from props to class strings. Libraries such as `cva` (class-variance-authority) formalise this. Two helpers are widely used:

- `clsx` joins classes conditionally: `clsx("px-4", active && "bg-indigo-600")`.
- `tailwind-merge` resolves conflicts so overrides win: `twMerge("px-4 py-2", "px-6")` gives `"py-2 px-6"`. Without it, both `px-4` and `px-6` would be present and the winner would depend on stylesheet order, not on the order in the class attribute.

**@apply** inlines utilities into your own CSS: `.btn { @apply rounded-md px-4 py-2; }`. It's reasonable for HTML you don't control (CMS output, third-party widgets) or very small shared pieces. Overusing it recreates traditional CSS, with naming and growing stylesheets, and gives up the benefits.

In v4, component style blocks (Vue `<style>`, Svelte, CSS modules) are processed separately, so `@apply` and theme variables there need `@reference "../app.css";` at the top, which imports the theme for reference without duplicating CSS.

Keep class order consistent with the Prettier plugin; it makes long lists far easier to scan.
takeaways: Extract components first; @apply second
Model component variants as maps from props to classes
tailwind-merge makes later conflicting classes win
Vue/Svelte style blocks need @reference to use @apply
pitfalls: Passing className="px-6" to a component that already has px-4 without merging; which one wins depends on CSS order.

quiz.q: Without tailwind-merge, an element has class="px-6 px-4". Which padding applies?
options: Whichever rule comes later in the generated stylesheet
px-6, because it comes first in the attribute
px-4, because it comes last in the attribute
quiz.explain: Class attribute order is irrelevant in CSS; stylesheet order and specificity decide.

concepts.name: Class detection and the build engine
concepts.summary: Know how v4's Rust-powered engine finds class names in your files, why dynamic class names fail, and how @source and safelisting work.
concepts.why: Missing styles in production almost always come from class names the scanner couldn't see.
concepts.body:
Tailwind doesn't run your code. Its engine (Oxide, written in Rust) scans files as **plain text**, extracting every token that could be a class name, and generates CSS for those that match a utility. Unknown tokens are ignored, so scanning is fast and over-inclusive rather than precise.

Consequences:

- Class names must appear **complete** in the source. `text-${color}-600` is never seen; map props to full strings instead: `{ red: "text-red-600", green: "text-green-600" }[color]`.
- Classes in comments or strings still generate CSS (harmless).
- Classes that only arrive at runtime, such as from a database or CMS, need to be listed somewhere the scanner looks.

**What gets scanned**: everything in the project except files in `.gitignore`, binary files, CSS files and lock files. The base path is the current working directory. Tools for edge cases:

- `@source "../node_modules/@acme/ui";` adds a path, such as a UI library in node_modules (ignored by default).
- `@source not "./legacy";` excludes a path.
- `@import "tailwindcss" source("../src");` sets the base path; `source(none)` disables automatic detection so only explicit `@source` paths are used, which suits monorepos.
- `@source inline("underline bg-red-{100..900..100}");` safelists classes, with brace expansion for ranges.

The build runs incrementally: only changed files are rescanned and new utilities appended, which is why rebuilds take milliseconds. Output is then processed by Lightning CSS for vendor prefixes, nesting and minification.
takeaways: The scanner reads files as text: class names must appear complete
node_modules and .gitignore'd paths are skipped by default
@source adds or excludes paths; source() sets the base
@source inline() safelists classes
pitfalls: Constructing class names from string fragments and seeing styles only in development, when they happened to exist elsewhere.

quiz.q: A component renders className={`text-${tone}-600`}. Why are the colours missing?
options: Template literals are not allowed in JSX
The scanner only sees complete class names in source text
quiz.explain: Tailwind never executes code, so text-red-600 never appears in the source and isn't generated.

concepts.name: Layers, Preflight and specificity
concepts.summary: See how v4 organises its output into native cascade layers, how utilities override components, and how the important modifier works.
concepts.why: Understanding the generated CSS explains every 'why doesn't my class win?' question in Tailwind projects.
concepts.body:
Tailwind v4 emits native **cascade layers** in this order: `@layer theme, base, components, utilities;`.

- **theme**: the `:root` CSS variables for theme values in use.
- **base**: Preflight, the reset built on modern-normalize: margins removed, `box-sizing: border-box`, borders set to `0 solid`, images block-level, headings unstyled.
- **components**: empty by default; your own component classes go here via `@layer components { ... }`.
- **utilities**: every generated utility and `@utility` you define.

Because layer order beats specificity, any utility overrides any component class, however specific its selector. That's why `class="btn px-8"` reliably gets `px-8`.

**Unlayered CSS beats all layers.** Custom CSS written after the import without a `@layer` wrapper overrides utilities, which surprises people migrating from v3. Wrap such styles in a layer, typically `components`.

Utilities are mostly single-class selectors with equal specificity, so among utilities, generated order decides. Tailwind sorts them deliberately: shorthand before longhand (`px-4` after `p-2` so it wins), and variants after base utilities, with breakpoints ordered small to large.

The **important modifier** ends with `!`: `bg-red-500!` adds `!important`. And `@import "tailwindcss" important;` marks all utilities important, for embedding into pages with aggressive existing CSS.

v4 also registers some internal custom properties with `@property` (with types and initial values), which lets things like gradient stops and shadow colours compose and animate correctly.
takeaways: Layer order: theme, base, components, utilities
Utilities beat component classes regardless of specificity
Unlayered custom CSS beats all utilities: wrap it in a layer
The ! suffix (bg-red-500!) adds !important
pitfalls: Writing unlayered custom CSS in v4 and finding utility classes no longer override it.

quiz.q:
Custom CSS '.card p { margin: 0 }' is written after @import "tailwindcss" without @layer. What happens to

inside .card?
options: mt-4 wins because utilities always win
The unlayered rule wins, so margin-top is 0
The build fails with a conflict error
quiz.explain: Unlayered styles beat every cascade layer, including utilities.

concepts.name: Upgrading from v3 and browser support
concepts.summary: Migrate v3 projects with the official upgrade tool and know the renamed utilities, changed defaults and modern-browser requirements of v4.
concepts.why: Many codebases and tutorials are still v3; knowing the differences prevents subtle visual regressions.
concepts.body:
v4 is a rewrite with a CSS-first configuration. The official tool does most of a migration: `npx @tailwindcss/upgrade` (run it on a clean branch) updates dependencies, converts `tailwind.config.js` into `@theme` and CSS directives, and rewrites class names in templates.

What changes and why it matters:

- **Imports**: `@tailwind base; @tailwind components; @tailwind utilities;` becomes `@import "tailwindcss";`. The CLI and PostCSS plugin moved to `@tailwindcss/cli` and `@tailwindcss/postcss`.
- **Renamed scales**: the old unnamed `shadow`, `rounded` and `blur` are now `shadow-sm`, `rounded-sm` and `blur-sm`, and the old `-sm` versions became `-xs`. `outline-none` is `outline-hidden`; `flex-shrink-0` is `shrink-0`.
- **Removed**: `bg-opacity-*` and similar opacity utilities; use the `/50` modifier.
- **Changed defaults**: borders and dividers default to `currentColor` instead of gray-200; `ring` is 1px instead of 3px; placeholder text uses the current colour at 50%; buttons use `cursor: default`.
- **Syntax**: variants stack left to right, the important modifier moves to the end (`bg-red-500!`), and CSS-variable values use `bg-(--x)`. Use `var(--color-red-500)` in CSS instead of `theme()`.

**Browser support** is the one hard constraint. v4 relies on `@property`, cascade layers and `color-mix()`, so it needs Safari 16.4+, Chrome 111+ and Firefox 128+. Projects that must support older browsers should stay on v3.4.
concepts.code:
# Migrate a v3 project (on a clean git branch)
npx @tailwindcss/upgrade

# Typical class changes the tool rewrites:
#   shadow-sm        -> shadow-xs
#   shadow           -> shadow-sm
#   rounded          -> rounded-sm
#   outline-none     -> outline-hidden
#   flex-shrink-0    -> shrink-0
#   bg-opacity-50    -> bg-black/50  (merged into the colour)
#   !mt-0            -> mt-0!
#   bg-[--brand]     -> bg-(--brand)

# Default changes to review visually afterwards:
#   border  -> currentColor instead of gray-200 (add border-gray-200 where needed)
#   ring    -> 1px instead of 3px (use ring-3 for the old look)
git diff --stat
takeaways: Run npx @tailwindcss/upgrade on a clean branch
Unnamed scale steps shifted: shadow -> shadow-sm, shadow-sm -> shadow-xs
Borders default to currentColor and ring to 1px
v4 requires Safari 16.4+, Chrome 111+, Firefox 128+
pitfalls: Trusting the automated upgrade without visually checking borders and rings, whose defaults changed.

quiz.q: After upgrading, bare 'border' elements suddenly look dark. Why?
options: Dark mode is on by default
The default border colour is now currentColor instead of gray-200
quiz.explain: v4 aligned the border default with CSS, which uses currentColor.
